title: Conjecture 1.2 (Georgakopoulos–Papasoglu)
statement_text: For every graph $H$ and all $c\geq 0$, there exists $L,C\geq 0$, such that if a graph $G$ does not contain $H$ as a $c$-fat minor, then $G$ admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with no $H$ minor.
context_text: Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu proposed this as a converse to the observation that quasi-isometries preserve minor containment up to fat-ness. The conjecture was verified for $H\in\{K_3, K_{1,m}, K_{2,3}, K_4^-\}$ but subsequently disproved in general by Davies, Hickingbotham, Illingworth, and McCarty, whose counterexample $H$ contains a clique of size 15. The present paper proves a related but distinct 'coarse graph theory analogue' in which the conclusion is quasi-isometry to a graph of bounded line-width rather than to a graph with no $H$ minor.
paper_contribution: Proves a 'coarse graph theory analogue': for every finite tree $H$ and every $c$, there exist $k,L,C$ such that every graph not containing $H$ as a $c$-fat minor admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with line-width at most $k$; and proves the matching converse. This replaces 'no $H$ minor' with 'line-width $\leq k$' and is restricted to tree $H$, so it does not resolve Conjecture 1.2 itself.
notes: The paper explicitly labels this item 'False conjecture', since it was disproved in general by arXiv:2405.09383. The attributed year 2023 reflects the arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.07456; the journal publication appeared in Combinatorica 45 (2025).
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. III. Excluding a fat tree

title: Informal question: validity of Conjecture 1.2 for trees and planar graphs
statement_text: Is the Georgakopoulos–Papasoglu conjecture (for all $c\ge0$ there exist $L,C\ge0$ such that every graph $G$ that does not contain $H$ as a $c$-fat minor admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with no $H$ minor) true when $H$ is a tree, or more generally when $H$ is a planar graph?
context_text: Graphs may be infinite and have no loops or parallel edges; distances are shortest-path distances. A map $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry if $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)+C$ and $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))+C$ whenever these distances are finite, and every vertex of $H$ is within distance $C$ of $\phi(V(G))$. $G$ contains $H$ as a $c$-fat minor if there are pairwise vertex-disjoint non-null connected subgraphs $\eta(x)$ of $G$, one for each vertex and each edge $x$ of $H$, such that for each edge $uv$ of $H$ there are edges of $G$ from $\eta(uv)$ to $\eta(u)$ and to $\eta(v)$, and $\mathrm{dist}_G(\eta(x),\eta(y))>c$ for all distinct $x,y$ except when one is a vertex of $H$ incident with the other, an edge. If $G$ contains $H$ as a $c$-fat minor with $c\ge L(L+C)+C$, then every graph to which $G$ is $(L,C)$-quasi-isometric contains $H$ as a minor; Georgakopoulos and Papasoglu conjectured the converse for every $H$. It is known for $H=K_3$ (Manning), $K_{1,m}$, $K_{2,3}$, $K_4^-$ and $K_{2,t}$, but was disproved in general by Davies, Hickingbotham, Illingworth and McCarty, and also for the octahedron by Albrechtsen, Distel and Georgakopoulos. In the version of the paper examined, the authors say it may be true for all trees $H$ as far as they know. Their main result is a coarse analogue of the Robertson–Seymour path-width theorem: for every finite tree $H$ there is $k$ such that for every $c$ there are $L,C$ such that every graph with no $c$-fat $H$-minor is $(L,C)$-quasi-isometric to a graph of line-width at most $k$ (line-width extends path-width to infinite graphs via decompositions indexed by a linear order), and conversely. This does not settle the conjecture for trees, whose conclusion asks for a quasi-isometric graph with no $H$ minor.
notes: Appears as a parenthetical remark in the introduction rather than a formally labelled environment.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. III. Excluding a fat tree
